before.content_html:
The Meaning and Significance of Peace

Peace is more than simply the absence of war. For religious believers, peace refers to a deep sense of harmony — between individuals, communities and nations. Both Christianity and Islam teach that peace is a central goal of human life and that believers have a duty to work towards it.

Christians believe that Jesus taught a message of peace throughout his ministry. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). This teaching shows that God values those who actively work to create peace, not simply those who avoid conflict.

In Islam, one of Allah’s 99 names is As-Salaam, meaning “the source of peace.” Muslims greet each other with “salaam alaikum” — “peace be upon you” — reinforcing the idea that peace is woven into everyday Muslim life. The Qur’an teaches that Allah created humanity to live in peace and harmony.

Key Fact

Christianity: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). Islam: One of Allah’s 99 names is As-Salaam (“the source of peace”). Both religions teach that peace is a central value and that believers should work actively to promote it.

Justice, Forgiveness and Reconciliation

Justice means ensuring fairness and upholding what is morally right. Religious believers see justice as a divine quality — God is just, and humans should reflect this in their treatment of others. Christians believe that God commands justice: “Act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8). In Islam, the Qur’an repeatedly instructs Muslims to act justly, even towards those they dislike: “Be just; that is nearer to righteousness” (Qur’an 5:8).

Forgiveness is the act of pardoning someone who has done wrong and choosing not to hold resentment. Christianity places forgiveness at the heart of its teaching. Jesus said: “If you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you” (Matthew 6:14). On the cross, Jesus prayed: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

In Islam, Allah is described as “the most merciful” (Ar-Rahman) and “the most forgiving” (Al-Ghaffar). Muslims are encouraged to forgive others because Allah forgives those who forgive. The Qur’an teaches: “Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah” (42:40).

Key Fact

Reconciliation goes beyond forgiveness — it means restoring a broken relationship and rebuilding trust. While forgiveness is a personal decision, reconciliation requires both sides to work together. Christians see reconciliation as central to their faith: God reconciled humanity to himself through Jesus’s death on the cross (2 Corinthians 5:18–19).

Violence means using physical force to cause harm. Some people use violent protest to try to bring about political or social change — for example, fighting with police, destroying property or setting off explosives. UK law allows peaceful protest but prohibits violent protest.

Christianity teaches non-violence. Jesus instructed his followers: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also” (Matthew 5:39). However, some Christians accept that violence may sometimes be a last resort when all peaceful options have failed. In Islam, violence is generally forbidden, but the Qur’an permits self-defence: “Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms” (Qur’an 22:39).

Terrorism is the use of violence against innocent people to create fear and force political change. It is condemned by all mainstream religious traditions. Christianity teaches that every human life is sacred (“sanctity of life”), and Islam states: “Do not take life, which God has made sacred” (Qur’an 6:151).

Some extremist groups claim religious justification for terrorism, but the vast majority of religious believers reject this. Malala Yousafzai, a Muslim education activist shot by the Taliban, demonstrated that faith inspires peace, not violence: “With guns you can kill terrorists, with education you can kill terrorism.” Nelson Mandela, a Christian, spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid through protest rather than terrorism.

Contrasting Beliefs on Violence

Christians and Muslims share many views on violence, but there are important differences in emphasis. Most Christians follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” and believe violence should be avoided wherever possible. The Quaker tradition (Society of Friends) takes an absolute pacifist stance, rejecting all forms of violence.

In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle in defence of Islam, but only under strict conditions — it must be declared by a legitimate authority, be proportionate, and be a last resort. The majority of Muslims reject violence as a tool for spreading faith, emphasising that “there is no compulsion in religion” (Qur’an 2:256). The key contrast is that Christianity has a stronger tradition of absolute pacifism (through groups like the Quakers), while Islam more explicitly permits defensive violence under strict conditions — but both religions agree that peace should always be the primary goal.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the meaning of 'reconciliation'?

A) Punishing someone for wrongdoing
B) Restoring harmony between people who have been in conflict
C) Using violence to achieve a political goal
D) Following the rules of a just war
practice_questions.marks: B) Restoring harmony between people who have been in conflict [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two religious teachings about peace.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct teaching, up to 2 marks. Answers may include:
• 'Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God' (Matthew 5:9)
• As-Salaam is one of Allah's 99 names, meaning 'the source of peace'
• Muslims greet each other with 'salaam alaikum' (peace be upon you)
• Jesus taught 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you' (Matthew 5:44)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two similar religious beliefs in contemporary British society about forgiveness.
In your answer you must refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include two of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity teaches that forgiveness is essential — Jesus said 'If you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you' (Matthew 6:14). Forgiveness is a duty for Christians.
• Similarly, Islam teaches that forgiveness brings reward from Allah — 'Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah' (Qur'an 42:40). Muslims are encouraged to forgive because Allah is 'the most forgiving'.
• Both religions teach that forgiveness can lead to reconciliation and the restoration of relationships.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about why violence is wrong.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — Jesus taught 'If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also' (Matthew 5:39), showing that Christians should not respond to violence with more violence. This reflects the broader Christian teaching that peace and love should guide all human actions.
• Islam — the Qur'an teaches 'Do not take life, which God has made sacred' (6:151), showing that Muslims believe human life has a God-given value that violence violates. While self-defence is permitted, unprovoked violence is forbidden.
• Source of authority: the Sermon on the Mount (Christianity) / the Qur'an (Islam) as a direct revelation from God.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'There is no difference between the Christian and Muslim attitudes to violence.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious arguments
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Both religions teach that peace is a core value — Christianity through Jesus's teaching on peacemaking, Islam through Allah's name As-Salaam.
• Both condemn terrorism and the targeting of innocent civilians.
• Both accept that violence may be justified in extreme circumstances, such as self-defence or as a last resort.
• Both teach the sanctity of life — violence against innocent people is always wrong.

Arguments against:
• Christianity has a stronger pacifist tradition — Jesus taught 'turn the other cheek' and the Quakers reject all violence absolutely.
• Islam permits armed struggle (lesser jihad) under strict conditions, which goes further than most Christian traditions in accepting the use of force.
• The concept of lesser jihad has no direct equivalent in mainstream Christianity.
• Some Christians argue that the Old Testament shows God supporting violence, while others reject this as outdated.

Conclusion: While there are significant similarities in their commitment to peace and condemnation of unjustified violence, there are genuine differences in how each religion frames the conditions under which force may be acceptable.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about reconciliation.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — Christians believe that God reconciled humanity to himself through the death of Jesus on the cross. St Paul wrote: 'God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ' (2 Corinthians 5:19). This shows that reconciliation is at the heart of the Christian faith.
• Islam — the Qur'an teaches 'Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah' (42:40). Muslims believe that restoring broken relationships pleases Allah and that reconciliation is a form of worship.
• Source of authority: the Bible / the Qur'an as the word of God.
[6 marks]

lessons.title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism

before.content_html:
Reasons for War

War is an armed conflict between two or more sides, usually nations or organised groups. There are many reasons why wars begin, but the three main reasons studied in GCSE Religious Studies are greed, self-defence and retaliation.

Greed drives wars fought for power, territory or resources. Many governments disguise greed as other motivations, but religious believers generally consider greed an unjust reason for war. Self-defence is widely accepted as a legitimate reason for fighting — both Christians and Muslims agree that protecting yourself and others from harm is justified. Retaliation means fighting back as revenge for a previous attack. While it can deter future aggression, religious believers warn that retaliation often creates a cycle of violence.

Just War Theory

The just war theory draws on the work of St Thomas Aquinas, who in the 13th century (Summa Theologiae II-II Q40) gave three conditions: just cause, right intention, and legitimate authority. The fuller seven-criteria version used today comes from the 1992 Catholic Catechism (CCC 2309), which added last resort, reasonable chance of success, proportional force, and civilian protection. It recognises that while peace is always preferable, there are circumstances where war may be the lesser evil.

Key Fact

The criteria for a just war include: (1) it must be fought for a just cause, such as self-defence; (2) it must be declared by a legitimate authority, such as a government; (3) the intention must be to promote good and overcome evil; (4) war must be a last resort, after all peaceful alternatives have been exhausted; (5) there must be a reasonable chance of success; (6) proportional force must be used — no more violence than is necessary; (7) civilians must not be deliberately targeted.

Most mainstream Christian denominations accept the just war theory. The Catholic Church teaches that governments have a right and duty to defend their citizens, provided the strict conditions of a just war are met. The Church of England also supports the just war approach, arguing that there are times when failing to act would cause greater suffering.

However, Jesus’s own teaching emphasises peace and non-violence. He said: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44) and “All who draw the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). This creates a tension within Christianity between the ideal of peace and the practical reality that war may sometimes be necessary.

Holy War

A holy war is a war fought for a religious cause or believed to be commanded by God. In Christianity, the Crusades (11th–13th centuries) are the most well-known example — European Christians fought to recapture the Holy Land from Muslim control. In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, but only under strict conditions.

For a holy war to be legitimate in Islam, it must be declared by a recognised religious authority, be fought in self-defence (not aggression), use proportionate force, and not target civilians, the elderly, women or children. The Qur’an states: “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not like transgressors” (2:190).

Key Fact

Just war vs holy war: A just war uses moral criteria to decide if a war is acceptable — it does not have to be religious. A holy war is fought specifically for a religious cause. Today, most Christian and Muslim leaders reject the idea of holy war, arguing that religion should not be used to justify violence.

Pacifism

Pacifism is the belief that all violence and war is wrong, regardless of the circumstances. Pacifists argue that conflicts should always be resolved through dialogue, negotiation and peaceful protest.

The strongest pacifist tradition in Christianity comes from the Quakers (Society of Friends), who believe that all war is wrong. They follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” (Matthew 5:39) literally and refuse to fight in any conflict. Many Quakers served as conscientious objectors during the World Wars, working as ambulance drivers or in hospitals instead.

Islam does not have a strong pacifist tradition in the same way. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad himself participated in battles to protect the early Muslim community. However, many Muslims emphasise that Islam means “peace” and that the greater jihad — the internal struggle to be a good Muslim — is more important than any physical conflict.

Religion as a Cause of War

Religion has been cited as a cause of conflict throughout history — from the Crusades to modern-day conflicts in the Middle East. However, many scholars argue that religion is rarely the sole cause of war. Most conflicts involve a complex mix of political, economic and territorial factors, with religion sometimes used to justify violence rather than being its root cause.

Both Christians and Muslims argue that their faith promotes peace, not war. Where religious violence occurs, leaders from both traditions condemn it. Pope Francis has stated that “war is always a defeat for humanity,” and Muslim scholars worldwide have signed declarations condemning violence carried out in the name of Islam.

Christianity: Quakers take an absolute pacifist position, rejecting all violence. Most other Christian denominations accept that war may sometimes be necessary (just war theory) but should always be a last resort. All Christians agree that Jesus taught peace and non-violence as the ideal.

Islam: Most Muslims are not pacifists in the absolute sense. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad fought to protect the Muslim community. However, peace is the preferred state, and the greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) is considered more important than the lesser jihad (armed conflict). Some individual Muslims, such as Abdul Ghaffar Khan, have adopted pacifist positions inspired by their faith.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'pacifism'?

A) The belief that war is acceptable if fought for God
B) The belief that all violence and war is wrong
C) The belief that only defensive wars are acceptable
D) The belief that violence is acceptable as a last resort
practice_questions.marks: B) The belief that all violence and war is wrong [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two criteria of the just war theory.
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each correct criterion, up to 2 marks. Answers may include:
• It must be fought for a just cause
• It must be declared by a legitimate authority
• The intention must be to promote good and overcome evil
• It must be a last resort
• There must be a reasonable chance of success
• Proportional force must be used
• Civilians must not be deliberately targeted
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting religious beliefs in contemporary British society about pacifism.
In your answer you must refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include two of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — Quakers (Society of Friends) believe in absolute pacifism. They follow Jesus's teaching to 'turn the other cheek' (Matthew 5:39) literally and refuse to fight in any war. This shows a tradition within Christianity that rejects all violence.
• Islam — most Muslims are not absolute pacifists. The Qur'an permits self-defence: 'Fight in the way of God those who fight you' (2:190). Muhammad participated in battles to defend the Muslim community. However, peace is always preferred.
• Most mainstream Christian denominations (Catholic, Anglican) accept just war theory, which means they are not absolute pacifists either, but accept war only as a last resort.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about when war may be justified.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — the just war theory, developed by St Thomas Aquinas, states that war is justified if it meets strict criteria such as just cause, legitimate authority and proportional force. Jesus also said 'All who draw the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:52), warning against unnecessary violence, but the Church accepts that self-defence may be necessary.
• Islam — the Qur'an states 'Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms' (22:39), showing that self-defence is a legitimate reason for war. The lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, but the response must be proportionate: 'If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate' (Qur'an).
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious believers should always be pacifists.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious arguments
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Jesus taught 'Blessed are the peacemakers' and 'turn the other cheek' — these teachings suggest Christians should always choose peace over violence.
• Quakers demonstrate that it is possible to be an absolute pacifist and still serve others during wartime (ambulance drivers, hospital workers).
• One meaning of Islam is 'peace', and the greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) is more important than the lesser jihad (armed conflict).
• Violence creates cycles of retaliation — pacifism breaks this cycle.

Arguments against:
• Most Christian denominations accept just war theory, recognising that sometimes failing to fight causes more suffering (e.g. allowing genocide).
• Islam permits self-defence — the Qur'an says 'Those who have been attacked are permitted to take up arms.' Refusing to defend yourself goes against this teaching.
• Pacifism may be unrealistic when faced with threats like terrorism or invasion.
• Some argue that fighting to protect the innocent is itself a moral duty, not a failure of faith.

Conclusion: While religious teachings clearly value peace, most believers accept that absolute pacifism is difficult to maintain when faced with extreme threats. The just war tradition offers a middle ground.
[12 marks] [plus spelling/grammar 3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about holy war.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include some of the following points, but all other relevant points must be credited:
• Christianity — the Crusades were fought as holy wars to recapture the Holy Land. The Pope at the time declared this a duty for Christians. However, most modern Christians reject the concept of holy war, believing that religion should never be used to justify violence. Jesus said 'Love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44).
• Islam — the lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, which some consider a form of holy war. The Qur'an states: 'Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress' (2:190). However, this is strictly defensive and must be proportionate. Most Muslim leaders reject the term 'holy war' as a misrepresentation of jihad.
[6 marks]

before.content_html:
Nuclear Weapons and Weapons of Mass Destruction

Weapons of mass destruction (WMDs) are weapons that can kill huge numbers of people and cause devastation over a wide area. The three main types are nuclear weapons, biological weapons (using disease) and chemical weapons (using poisonous substances). The use of WMDs is one of the most controversial moral issues in modern warfare.

Nuclear weapons are the most powerful WMDs ever created. The atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945 killed over 200,000 people, many of them civilians. The long-term effects included radiation sickness, birth defects and environmental destruction that lasted for decades. Today, several countries possess nuclear arsenals, and the threat of nuclear war remains a global concern.

Key Fact

Nuclear weapons violate several criteria of the just war theory: they cannot be used proportionately (their destructive power is too great), they inevitably target civilians (blast radius is indiscriminate), and their long-term effects (radiation, environmental damage) extend far beyond the battlefield. For these reasons, most religious believers oppose their use.

Nuclear Deterrence

Nuclear deterrence is the idea that possessing nuclear weapons prevents war because no nation would risk attacking a country that could retaliate with nuclear force. This was the basis of the Cold War strategy of “mutually assured destruction” (MAD) — if both sides would be destroyed, neither side would start a war.

Arguments for deterrence: Nuclear weapons have arguably prevented major wars between nuclear powers since 1945. The threat of mutual destruction makes war too costly to consider. Some argue that giving up nuclear weapons unilaterally would leave a country vulnerable to attack or nuclear blackmail.

Arguments against deterrence: The threat to use weapons that would kill millions of civilians is itself immoral. Deterrence relies on the willingness to commit mass murder, which contradicts the sanctity of life. Accidents, miscalculations or rogue states could lead to nuclear war regardless of deterrence. The money spent on nuclear weapons could be used to address poverty and suffering.

Contrasting Beliefs on WMDs

Christianity: Most Christian denominations oppose the use of nuclear weapons. The Catholic Church has called for complete nuclear disarmament, and Pope Francis has stated that even the possession of nuclear weapons is “to be condemned.” Jesus’s teaching to “love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44) and the principle of sanctity of life make the mass killing caused by nuclear weapons incompatible with Christian ethics. However, some Christians support nuclear deterrence as a way of preventing war, arguing that the intention is peace, not destruction.

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that war must be proportionate — “If you have to respond to an attack, make your response proportionate” (Qur’an). Nuclear weapons are inherently disproportionate and indiscriminate, violating this principle. Islam also forbids the killing of innocent civilians, which makes the use of WMDs incompatible with Islamic teachings. However, some Muslim-majority countries possess nuclear weapons, arguing that deterrence protects their people from aggression.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam oppose the use of weapons of mass destruction. The key area of debate is possession for deterrence. Some believers argue that possessing nuclear weapons prevents greater harm; others argue that even the threat of using them is morally wrong because it relies on the willingness to kill millions of innocent people.

Peacemaking and the Work of Individuals

Religious teachings have inspired many individuals and organisations to work for peace. Peacemaking involves actively working to resolve conflicts, support victims and prevent future violence. Both Christianity and Islam teach that believers have a duty to pursue peace.

Desmond Tutu was an Anglican archbishop in South Africa who led the fight against apartheid through peaceful means. Inspired by Jesus’s teachings on love and reconciliation, he chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission after apartheid ended, helping victims and perpetrators to find a path to forgiveness. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1984.

Malala Yousafzai, a Muslim from Pakistan, campaigned for girls’ right to education despite death threats from the Taliban. After being shot in the head in 2012, she continued her work, saying: “With guns you can kill terrorists, with education you can kill terrorism.” Her faith in Allah’s plan sustained her through her recovery. She became the youngest-ever Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 2014.

Religious Responses to Victims of War

Religious organisations play a vital role in supporting victims of war around the world. They provide humanitarian aid, shelter, medical care, education and emotional support to refugees and displaced people.

Islamic Relief Worldwide was founded in Birmingham, UK, in 1984. Inspired by the Islamic principle of zakah (charitable giving), it provides emergency relief and long-term development support to victims of war and conflict worldwide. In recent years, it has responded to crises in Syria, Yemen, Gaza and Afghanistan, providing food, clean water, medical care and shelter to millions of displaced people.

Islamic Relief’s work is motivated by the Qur’anic teaching: “Whoever saves a life, it is as if he has saved the whole of humanity” (5:32). The organisation works across religious boundaries, helping people of all faiths and none. This reflects the Islamic belief in the universal value of human life and the duty to help those in need, regardless of their background.

Other religious organisations involved in supporting victims of war include Christian Aid, CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development), and the Red Cross (founded on Christian principles of compassion). These organisations demonstrate that religious teachings on peace, justice and compassion are not just theoretical — they inspire practical action to help those suffering from the effects of conflict.
